name: travel-agent-gym
description: A Gymnasium RL environment for an AI travel agent: interview a client with hidden preferences, search, plan, book, then survive the trip's disruptions.

readme.html:
travel-agent-gym

A client writes in: "family of four, Japan in spring, around $4k." They do not mention that one of them uses a wheelchair, or that food matters to them more than anything else. A good travel agent finds that out before booking. A bad one books the cheapest flight and the best-rated hotel, and the trip falls apart in week two.

This repository is a reinforcement-learning environment built around that job. An agent interviews a client whose preferences are hidden, searches inventory, builds an itinerary that has to fit a real clock, books it against a budget, and then the trip actually happens and a disruption engine fires. The reward is the trip the client actually got, not the plan.

It is a Gymnasium environment, so a standard RL algorithm (MaskablePPO here) can train on it, and the same action set is rendered as tool calls so an LLM agent can play it too.

Status, plainly: the first world (v1) turned out too easy. The second world (v2) fixed the part that mattered and then overshot: today it is too hard for the reasons explained in Where v2 overshot. Both worlds run. The 98 tests cover v1; v2 has its baselines and a world-coherence check. The numbers below are re-measured from this code.

What happens in one episode

 Act I: plan and book                                   Act II: the trip
 ─────────────────────────────────────────────────      ──────────────────────────────
 client's opening line (reveals 1-3 of 8 preferences)
        │
        ▼
 INTERVIEW ──► ask about preferences and the party      disruption engine fires, but
        │      (patience drops every turn)              only on what was booked:
        ▼
 SEARCH ─────► slates of up to 8 options                  flight delayed
        │      (flights, rail, ferries, hotels,             └► missed connection
        │       activities; filters, not sort orders)           └► late arrival
        ▼                                                          └► hotel no-show
 ITINERARY ──► every segment must fit the clock:
        │      a.end + transfer(a, b) <= b.start        a cheap non-refundable fare with
        ▼                                               a 45-minute connection now costs
 BOOK ───────► integer-cent ledger; overspending        what it really costs
        │      is not penalised, it is impossible
        ▼                                                         │
 FINALIZE ──────────────────────────────────────────────►  terminal reward
Part What it does Where
Interview The client has eight hidden preference weights (cost, comfort, location, pacing, food, culture, novelty, reliability) and, in v2, a hidden party: each traveller's age, passport, access needs and diet. Patience runs down every turn, and the client can walk out. travel_env/personas.py, personas_v2.py, client_sim.py
Search Each search returns a fixed-width slate of candidates, and the agent selects by index. Presets are different candidate sets, not different sort orders. travel_env/actions.py, actions_v2.py
Itinerary One inequality on a timeline replaces a pile of special cases: over-packed days, moving cities without a booked leg, a tour that starts before the flight lands. travel_env/timeline.py, itinerary.py, clock.py
Booking An authoritative ledger in integer cents. Illegal actions (over budget, wrong city, museum closed that day) are removed by the action mask, never punished. travel_env/ledger.py, env_v2.py
Disruption engine Act II runs the booked trip. Delays, cancellations, overbooking, weather and strikes fire conditionally on what was booked, and a delay cascades through the timeline as far as it really reaches. travel_env/disruptions.py, env_v2.py

Two worlds

v1 (travel_agent/TravelAgent-v0) v2 (travel_agent/TravelAgent-v2, the default)
Geography Tokyo, Kyoto, Osaka; 14 hand-set districts Japan, Italy, Thailand; 13 cities, 43 districts; one or two regions per episode (two means an open-jaw route)
Transport flights and one rail corridor flight, rail, bus, ferry, car hire on local timetables; Thailand's ferries cancel in the monsoon
Lodging hotels 7 types (hotel, ryokan, hostel, apartment, capsule, resort, guesthouse) with real occupancy rules
Time had three silent timezone bugs UTC offsets from zoneinfo, arrivals derived from distance; clock.assert_world_coherent checks every instant, leg and duration (it passes on 50 generated worlds, but the tests do not run it yet)
Travel times a haversine rule 108 real Google Distance Matrix pairs, fetched once into data/transfer_matrix.json; nothing calls the network inside step()
Hard constraints none accessibility, capacity and documents: masked once the agent has asked, unmasked (and fatal at travel time) if it has not
Actions Discrete(63) Discrete(89)

v1 is kept, unchanged, because its trained checkpoint (models/v1_ppo/) is the evidence that the reward carries a learnable signal.

The synthetic world is correlated on purpose. Price tracks a hotel's true quality plus noise. Displayed ratings are noisier when a hotel has few reviews, so sorting by rating picks lucky small-sample hotels and overpays (measured over 200 worlds in data/world_stats.md). The cheap, well-located seats and rooms are often the ones already gone. A sample world and ten sample clients, hidden weights included, are in data/.

Reward

per turn:   Φ(s_t) − Φ(s_{t−1})  −  friction
terminal:   realised client utility + budget efficiency − disruption damage − patience forfeit

The shaping term is a potential difference, with Φ = 0 at termination and at truncation, so it cannot change which policy is optimal. There is no LLM anywhere in the reward: it is integer arithmetic over the ledger, and the same seed gives the same reward. Every component is reported separately in info.

The two obvious exploits score zero without a penalty term written against either:

Exploit Why it loses
Always book the cheapest flight Act II makes cheap and fragile lose in expectation
Always pick the highest-rated hotel Ratings from few reviews are noisy, and price tracks real quality
Book without asking The weights are hidden, so an unasked booking is a bet on a prior
Ask forever Patience runs out and the client walks

Baselines

Six scripted policies. null does nothing. random picks uniformly among legal actions. greedy_cheapest and greedy_quality are the two exploits. heuristic interviews the client on preferences, then searches and books. expert (v2 only) is the heuristic plus four questions about the party's hard constraints.

v1, 24 seeds, from logs/published/baselines_v1.txt (python -m eval.harness 24):

policy             solve   return_iqm   complete   walk_rate   steps
null               0.00      -1.0097        0.00       0.67     50.5
random             0.125     -1.1405        0.25       0.83     30.6
greedy_cheapest    0.00      -1.3002        0.00       0.96     26.4
greedy_quality     0.00      -1.3115        0.00       0.96     26.4
heuristic          0.75      +0.1100        0.75       0.25     47.0

The committed MaskablePPO checkpoint solves 88% of 24 episodes (seeds 5000–5023) with mean return +0.126 (logs/published/v1_ppo_checkpoint_eval.txt). Its training run went from −1.02 to +0.133 mean episode reward over 516k steps, with a best evaluation of 0.36 ± 0.11 at 400k steps (logs/published/v1_ppo_train.log, lines 6, 3736 and 2901).

That is the problem with v1. Random solved one episode in eight and completed one in four, so the task could be finished by accident. A hand-written heuristic solved three in four, and a learned policy nearly nine in ten. My targets were random near zero and the heuristic near 30%: low enough that a learned policy has something to find, high enough that success is not so rare a learner never sees it. v1 missed both.

v2, 60 seeds, from logs/published/baselines_v2.txt (python eval/run_v2.py 60):

policy             solve   ret_iqm   complete   walk   steps   prefs   hard_q   cfail
null                0.00   -0.3600       0.00   0.00    90.0    0.33     0.00    0.00
random              0.00   -0.3782       0.00   0.13    89.5    0.91     0.99    0.00
greedy_cheapest     0.00   -1.7207       0.00   0.63    82.1    0.25     0.00    0.00
greedy_quality      0.00   -1.7230       0.00   0.63    82.1    0.25     0.00    0.00
heuristic           0.05   -1.3175       0.08   0.47    83.7    0.57     0.00    0.02
expert              0.02   -1.1827       0.03   0.42    85.0    0.57     1.00    0.00

prefs is the share of preference axes the policy found out; hard_q is the share of hard-constraint classes it asked about; cfail is the share of trips that broke a constraint at travel time.

Where v2 overshot

                 v1      v2      target
random          12.5%    0%      ~0%        fixed: no more solving by accident
heuristic       75%      5%      ~30%       overshot, and for the wrong reason

Random going to zero is the real win. A coherent multi-region route with a correct night-by-night allocation is not something a uniform policy stumbles into.

The heuristic at 5% is a failure, and not because the task became appropriately hard. Its complete is 0.08: it is failing to finish trips, not making bad choices. Steps sit at 82–90 against a 90-turn cap. Two causes were found and fixed during development (no budget reserve for the return leg, so one outbound flight could eat 97% of the budget, and a heuristic that repeated the same empty search). Completion is still low. Raising the turn cap from 90 to 150 made it worse, because patience then ran out first (the measurement is recorded next to MAX_TURNS in travel_env/env_v2.py).

Two consequences follow, and both are open:

  • Interviewing does not yet pay. expert asks about every hard constraint and scores inside noise of heuristic (2% against 5%), because neither finishes. v2's central idea is built, and this measurement does not yet show it working.
  • Doing nothing is the best policy. null scores −0.360 and heuristic −1.318: a policy that books a trip absorbs disruption damage and constraint failures, and one that stalls pays only the patience forfeit. PPO found this. Its training reward converged to −0.00005 with episodes running to 89.9 of 90 turns, so it never books (logs/published/v2_ppo_train.log, lines 4326–4327; the deterministic evaluation at 500k steps is −0.68 ± 0.65, line 4304). The curve goes up. What it climbs toward is inaction.

The fix order matters. Completion comes first: at 8% completion no reward shape saves this. Then the terminal needs rebalancing, because a PATIENCE_FORFEIT of 1.0 is cheap next to a DISRUPTION_SCALE of 0.9 applied to damage that can reach 2.0 (travel_env/rewards.py). Walking away should be the worst outcome, not a floor to retreat to.

A note on the history. Commit messages and earlier versions of this README record a v1 heuristic at 96% and a v2 heuristic at 7%. Re-running the committed code, on any seed count I tried and with the original library versions, gives 67–83% for v1 and 5% for v2; the "random solves 25%" figure came from the test suite's 12-seed sample. The tables above are the re-run (Linux x86-64, Python 3.12, NumPy 2.5, Gymnasium 1.4). The conclusions do not change.

The LLM path

travel_env/llm_agent.py turns the observation and action mask into tool schemas, so an LLM agent is only ever offered legal actions. travel_env/client_sim.py plays the client with an LLM whose context holds the persona as prose and the transcript, never the world, the ledger or the weights as numbers. Agent and client are independent switches, so all four combinations run, and --dry-run makes no network calls (logs/published/llm_eval_dryrun.json).

One short live run (two episodes, gpt-5-mini as the agent, gpt-4.1-mini as the client) found 91% of preference axes and asked about 100% of hard-constraint classes, against the heuristic's 57% and 0%, and still completed no trips. Its raw output was not saved; the numbers are in the commit "Fix the LLM eval call-budget bug; record the first working live run". An LLM doing the right thing and hitting the same wall points at the environment, not the agents.

Quick start

uv venv --python 3.12 .venv
uv pip install --python .venv/bin/python -e ".[train,dev]"

PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python scripts/smoke.py            # one rendered episode
PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python -m eval.harness 24          # v1 baseline table
PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python eval/run_v2.py 60           # v2 baseline table
PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python -m pytest tests             # 98 invariant tests (v1)
PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python scripts/play_trained.py     # watch the v1 checkpoint play
PYTHONPATH=. .venv/bin/python scripts/train.py --steps 400000 --n-envs 10

Everything above runs offline with no keys. Two optional paths need one: the LLM agent and client (LLM_API_KEY and LLM_BASE_URL for any OpenAI-compatible gateway, or OPENROUTER_API_KEY), and the one-off rebuild of the travel-time matrix (GOOGLE_MAPS_API_KEY). Copy .env.example to .env to set them.

Layout

Path Contents
travel_env/ the environments, world generators, contracts, ledger, timeline, reward, disruption engine, LLM adapters
eval/ baselines, the evaluation harness (solve rate, IQM return, pass^k), the LLM evaluation
scripts/ smoke test, training, checkpoint playback, data dumps, the travel-time fetcher
tests/ 98 invariant tests for v1 that drive the real environment, no mocks
data/ the travel-time matrix, a sample world, sample clients, measured world statistics
logs/published/, models/v1_ppo/ training logs, baseline outputs, the v1 checkpoint
